Prof Q/ ELEC 10314 problems
We’ll work through these together in class.
Problem 1
Ch. 1 — Scientific and Engineering Notation
A high-value resistor measures $4\,700\,000\ \Omega$. Express this value in scientific notation and in engineering notation (exponent a multiple of 3). Then write it using the matching metric prefix.
Write $4\,700\,000\ \Omega$ in scientific notation, in engineering notation, and with a metric prefix.
$4.7 \times 10^{6}\ \Omega = 4.7\ \text{M}\Omega$ Ω
Step 1Given $R = 4\,700\,000\ \Omega$.
Step 2Scientific notation: move the decimal point 6 places left: $R = 4.7 \times 10^{6}\ \Omega$.
Step 3Engineering notation: 6 is a multiple of 3, so the form is unchanged: $4.7 \times 10^{6}\ \Omega$.
Step 4The prefix for $10^{6}$ is mega: $$R = 4.7\ \text{M}\Omega$$
Worked Solution
Given: $R = 4\,700\,000\ \Omega$. Scientific notation: move the decimal point 6 places left so one nonzero digit is before it, giving $R = 4.7 \times 10^{6}\ \Omega$. Engineering notation: the exponent 6 is already a multiple of 3, so the engineering form is the same, $4.7 \times 10^{6}\ \Omega$. The prefix for $10^{6}$ is mega (M): $$R = 4.7 \times 10^{6}\ \Omega = 4.7\ \text{M}\Omega$$
Problem 2
Ch. 1 — Metric-Prefix Conversion
A sensor's output current is specified as $0.068\ \text{mA}$. Your data sheet template requires the value in microamperes. Convert $0.068\ \text{mA}$ to $\mu\text{A}$, showing the powers of ten you use.
Convert $0.068\ \text{mA}$ to $\mu\text{A}$.
68 µA
Step 1Given $I = 0.068\ \text{mA}$, with milli $= 10^{-3}$ and micro $= 10^{-6}$.
Step 2Convert to amperes: $I = 0.068 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 6.8 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{A}$.
Step 3Divide by $10^{-6}$ for microamperes: $$I = \frac{6.8 \times 10^{-5}}{10^{-6}}\ \mu\text{A} = 68\ \mu\text{A}$$
Step 4Check: a smaller prefix gives a larger number, since $0.068 \times 10^{3} = 68$.
Worked Solution
Given: $I = 0.068\ \text{mA}$. Prefix values: milli $= 10^{-3}$ and micro $= 10^{-6}$. Convert to amperes: $I = 0.068 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 6.8 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{A}$. Convert to microamperes by dividing by $10^{-6}$: $$I = \frac{6.8 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{A}}{10^{-6}\ \text{A}/\mu\text{A}} = 6.8 \times 10^{1}\ \mu\text{A} = 68\ \mu\text{A}$$ Check: micro is $10^{3}$ times smaller than milli, so the number grows by $10^{3}$: $0.068 \times 1\,000 = 68$.
Problem 3
Ch. 1 — Significant Figures in Multi-Step Calculations
Two cells are connected in series, aiding. Their measured voltages are $5.13\ \text{V}$ and $1.2\ \text{V}$. A charge of $0.0240\ \text{C}$ moves through both cells. The energy delivered is $W = V_T\, Q$, where $V_T$ is the sum of the cell voltages. Find $W$ and report it with the correct number of significant figures. Carry unrounded intermediate values, and state which rule and which measurement limits each step.
Find $V_T$, then the energy $W$ in joules, reported to the correct significant figures.
0.15 J
Step 1Given $V_1 = 5.13\ \text{V}$, $V_2 = 1.2\ \text{V}$, $Q = 0.0240\ \text{C}$.
Step 2Add: $V_T = 5.13 + 1.2 = 6.33\ \text{V}$.
Step 3Addition rule: $1.2\ \text{V}$ limits the sum to tenths, so $V_T \approx 6.3\ \text{V}$ (2 sig figs). Keep 6.33 as a guard digit.
Step 4Multiply: $$W = (6.33\ \text{V})(0.0240\ \text{C}) = 0.151\,92\ \text{J}$$
Step 5Multiplication rule: 2 sig figs is the fewest, so $W = 0.15\ \text{J}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $V_1 = 5.13\ \text{V}$, $V_2 = 1.2\ \text{V}$, $Q = 0.0240\ \text{C}$. Step 1 (addition, where the least precise decimal place governs): $V_T = 5.13 + 1.2 = 6.33\ \text{V}$. The value $1.2\ \text{V}$ is known only to the tenths place, so $V_T$ is good to $6.3\ \text{V}$, which is 2 significant figures. Keep 6.33 as a guard value. Step 2 (multiplication, where the fewest significant figures govern): $$W = V_T\, Q = (6.33\ \text{V})(0.0240\ \text{C}) = 0.151\,92\ \text{J}$$ Units: $\text{V}\cdot\text{C} = (\text{J/C})\cdot\text{C} = \text{J}$. $V_T$ has 2 significant figures and $Q$ has 3, so $W$ keeps 2: $$W = 0.15\ \text{J}$$
Problem 4
Ch. 1 — Unit Conversion
A test shows that a battery delivered a total charge of $36\,000\ \text{C}$. Battery capacities are usually stated in ampere-hours. Using $1\ \text{C} = 1\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$ and $1\ \text{h} = 3\,600\ \text{s}$, express this charge in ampere-hours.
Convert $36\,000\ \text{C}$ to ampere-hours.
10 A·h
Step 1Given $Q = 36\,000\ \text{C} = 36\,000\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$.
Step 2Choose the factor $\frac{1\ \text{h}}{3\,600\ \text{s}}$ so that seconds cancel.
Step 3Multiply: $$Q = 36\,000 \times \frac{1}{3\,600}\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h} = 10\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h}$$
Step 4Equivalently, $Q = 10\,000\ \text{mAh}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $Q = 36\,000\ \text{C} = 36\,000\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$. Multiply by a conversion factor equal to 1 that cancels seconds: $$Q = 36\,000\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s} \times \frac{1\ \text{h}}{3\,600\ \text{s}} = 10\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h}$$ Equivalently, $Q = 10\,000\ \text{mAh}$.
Problem 5
Ch. 1 — Reported Precision and Uncertainty
A handheld meter displays $12.3478\ \text{V}$ across a power-supply output. Its accuracy specification on this range is $\pm 0.8\%$ of the reading. Compute the uncertainty and round it to one significant figure. Then report the voltage in the form value $\pm$ uncertainty, keeping only the digits the uncertainty justifies.
Report the voltage with appropriate precision in the form $V \pm \Delta V$.
12.3 ± 0.1 V
Step 1Given $V = 12.3478\ \text{V}$ with accuracy $\pm 0.8\%$ of reading.
Step 2Compute the uncertainty: $\Delta V = 0.008 \times 12.3478 = 0.0988\ \text{V}$.
Step 3Round the uncertainty to one significant figure: $\Delta V \approx 0.1\ \text{V}$, in the tenths place.
Step 4Round the reading to the same place: $12.3478 \rightarrow 12.3\ \text{V}$.
Step 5Report: $$V = 12.3 \pm 0.1\ \text{V}$$
Worked Solution
Given: reading $V = 12.3478\ \text{V}$ and accuracy $\pm 0.8\%$ of reading. Uncertainty: $$\Delta V = 0.008 \times 12.3478\ \text{V} = 0.0988\ \text{V}$$ Rounded to one significant figure: $\Delta V \approx 0.1\ \text{V}$. The uncertainty is in the tenths place, so round the reading to the tenths: $12.3478 \rightarrow 12.3\ \text{V}$. Reported result: $$V = 12.3 \pm 0.1\ \text{V}$$ The display shows six digits, but only three are meaningful.
Problem 6
Ch. 1 — Calculations in Powers of Ten
Without converting to ordinary decimals, evaluate $$X = \frac{(5.60 \times 10^{-4})^{2}(2.00 \times 10^{9})}{4.00 \times 10^{-2}}$$ Handle the coefficients and the powers of ten separately. Give the result in scientific notation and in engineering notation, and name the matching metric prefix. Report 3 significant figures.
Evaluate $X$ in scientific and engineering notation, and name the matching metric prefix.
$1.57 \times 10^{4} = 15.7 \times 10^{3}$ (kilo)
Step 1Square the first factor: $(5.60 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 31.36 \times 10^{-8} = 3.136 \times 10^{-7}$.
Step 2Multiply: $(3.136 \times 10^{-7})(2.00 \times 10^{9}) = 6.272 \times 10^{2}$.
Step 3Divide: $$X = \frac{6.272}{4.00} \times 10^{2-(-2)} = 1.568 \times 10^{4}$$
Step 4Round to 3 sig figs: $X = 1.57 \times 10^{4}$.
Step 5Engineering form: $15.7 \times 10^{3}$. The prefix is kilo, so $X = 15.7\ \text{k}$.
Worked Solution
Square the first factor: $(5.60)^2 = 31.36$ and $(10^{-4})^2 = 10^{-8}$, so $(5.60 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 31.36 \times 10^{-8} = 3.136 \times 10^{-7}$. Multiply by the second factor: $(3.136)(2.00) = 6.272$ and $10^{-7} \times 10^{9} = 10^{2}$, giving the numerator $6.272 \times 10^{2}$. Divide by the denominator: $$X = \frac{6.272}{4.00} \times 10^{2-(-2)} = 1.568 \times 10^{4}$$ Rounded to 3 significant figures: $X = 1.57 \times 10^{4}$. Engineering notation: $1.57 \times 10^{4} = 15.7 \times 10^{3}$. The prefix for $10^{3}$ is kilo (k), so $X = 15.7\ \text{k}$.
Problem 7
Ch. 2 — Charge and Current from an Electron Count
A total of $1.875 \times 10^{19}$ electrons pass a point in a conductor in $1.5\ \text{s}$. Using the constant $1\ \text{C} \approx 6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons and $I = Q/t$, find the charge in coulombs and the current in amperes.
Find the charge $Q$ and the current $I$.
2.0 A
Step 1Given $n = 1.875 \times 10^{19}$ electrons, $t = 1.5\ \text{s}$, and $1\ \text{C} = 6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.
Step 2Convert to charge: $$Q = \frac{1.875 \times 10^{19}}{6.25 \times 10^{18}} = 3.0\ \text{C}$$
Step 3Current: $$I = \frac{3.0\ \text{C}}{1.5\ \text{s}} = 2.0\ \text{A}$$
Step 4Interpretation: 2.0 coulombs pass the point every second.
Worked Solution
Given: $n = 1.875 \times 10^{19}$ electrons and $t = 1.5\ \text{s}$. Charge: $$Q = \frac{1.875 \times 10^{19}\ \text{electrons}}{6.25 \times 10^{18}\ \text{electrons/C}} = 0.30 \times 10^{1}\ \text{C} = 3.0\ \text{C}$$ Current: $$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{3.0\ \text{C}}{1.5\ \text{s}} = 2.0\ \text{A}$$ So 2.0 coulombs pass the point each second.
Problem 8
Ch. 2 — Resistor Color Code and Tolerance
A 4-band resistor has the bands red, red, orange, gold, read from left to right. The color code is: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. A gold fourth band means $\pm 5\%$ tolerance. Decode the nominal value and tolerance, and find the acceptable range. Give the maximum in-tolerance resistance as your final answer, and state whether a part measuring $23.4\ \text{k}\Omega$ passes.
Decode the resistor, find its tolerance range, give the maximum in-tolerance resistance in kilohms, and judge a $23.4\ \text{k}\Omega$ reading.
23.1 kΩ
Step 1Digit bands: red, red $= 2, 2$, giving 22.
Step 2Multiplier band, orange, is $10^{3}$: $R = 22 \times 10^{3} = 22\ \text{k}\Omega$.
Step 3Tolerance band, gold, means $\pm 5\%$: $\Delta R = 0.05 \times 22\,000 = 1\,100\ \Omega$.
Step 4Range: $$R_{\min} = 20.9\ \text{k}\Omega, \quad R_{\max} = 23.1\ \text{k}\Omega$$
Step 5Since $23.4\ \text{k}\Omega > 23.1\ \text{k}\Omega$, the part is out of tolerance.
Worked Solution
Digit bands: red $= 2$ and red $= 2$, giving 22. Multiplier band: orange $= 10^{3}$. Nominal: $R = 22 \times 10^{3}\ \Omega = 22\ \text{k}\Omega$. Tolerance band: gold $= \pm 5\%$, so $\Delta R = 0.05 \times 22\,000 = 1\,100\ \Omega$. Range: $$R_{\min} = 22\,000 - 1\,100 = 20\,900\ \Omega = 20.9\ \text{k}\Omega$$ $$R_{\max} = 22\,000 + 1\,100 = 23\,100\ \Omega = 23.1\ \text{k}\Omega$$ A reading of $23.4\ \text{k}\Omega$ is above $23.1\ \text{k}\Omega$, so the part is out of tolerance and fails.
Problem 9
Ch. 2 — DMM Ohmmeter Range, Resolution, and Accuracy
A manual-ranging $3\tfrac{1}{2}$-digit DMM (maximum display 1999 counts) has resistance ranges of 200 Ω, 2 kΩ, and 20 kΩ. It is used to measure an isolated resistor whose true resistance is $1\,527\ \Omega$. Determine what the display shows on each range, and choose the range with the best resolution. On that range, the accuracy specification is $\pm(0.8\%\ \text{of reading} + 2\ \text{counts})$. Compute the worst-case uncertainty of the reading in ohms.
DMM resistance ranges (3½-digit, 1999 counts)
Range     Max display   Resolution (1 count)
200 Ω     199.9 Ω       0.1 Ω
2 kΩ      1.999 kΩ      0.001 kΩ (1 Ω)
20 kΩ     19.99 kΩ      0.01 kΩ (10 Ω)
Find the display on each range, choose the best range, and compute the worst-case uncertainty in ohms.
14.2 Ω
Step 1200 Ω range: $1\,527\ \Omega > 199.9\ \Omega$, so the display shows OL.
Step 22 kΩ range: the resolution is $1\ \Omega$, so the display shows $1.527\ \text{k}\Omega$.
Step 320 kΩ range: the resolution is $10\ \Omega$, so the display shows $1.53\ \text{k}\Omega$.
Step 4Best range: 2 kΩ, the lowest range without overload.
Step 5Uncertainty: $$\Delta R = 0.008(1\,527) + 2(1) = 12.216 + 2 = 14.216\ \Omega$$
Step 6Result: $\Delta R \approx 14.2\ \Omega$, so the reading is $1.527\ \text{k}\Omega \pm 14\ \Omega$.
Worked Solution
200 Ω range: $1\,527\ \Omega$ exceeds $199.9\ \Omega$, so the display shows OL (overload). 2 kΩ range: the resolution is $1\ \Omega$, so the display shows $1.527\ \text{k}\Omega$. 20 kΩ range: the resolution is $10\ \Omega$, so the display shows $1.53\ \text{k}\Omega$. The best range is 2 kΩ, the lowest range without overload, which gives four significant digits. Uncertainty on the 2 kΩ range, where one count is $1\ \Omega$: $$\Delta R = 0.008 \times 1\,527\ \Omega + 2 \times 1\ \Omega = 12.216 + 2 = 14.216\ \Omega$$ So $\Delta R \approx 14.2\ \Omega$. The reading is $1.527\ \text{k}\Omega \pm 14\ \Omega$, so the true value lies between about $1\,513$ and $1\,541\ \Omega$.
Problem 10
Ch. 2 — Setting Up a Resistance Measurement
In a circuit, battery B1 feeds switch S1 and then two resistors, R1 and R2, which are connected in parallel between node A and node B. You must measure the resistance of R1 alone with a digital multimeter. Describe, in order, how you prepare the circuit and the meter. Explain why measuring directly across nodes A and B would not give the resistance of R1.
Circuit with R1 and R2 in parallel
Describe the preparation and meter setup for measuring R1 alone, and explain why a direct measurement across A and B is wrong.
(1) Open S1 and disconnect B1. Resistance must be measured with power removed, because the ohmmeter supplies its own small test current. (2) Disconnect at least one lead of R1 from the circuit to isolate it from R2. (3) Set the DMM to the resistance (Ω) function, with the black lead in COM and the red lead in V/Ω. (4) Touch the probes to the two ends of R1, avoiding contact with your fingers, and choose the lowest range that does not overload. (5) Read the value and compare it with the color code. Measuring across A and B with R2 still connected gives the parallel combination of R1 and R2, which is less than either resistor, not R1 alone.
Step 1An ohmmeter supplies its own test current, so the circuit must be unpowered and the component isolated.
Step 2Open S1 and disconnect B1.
Step 3Lift one lead of R1 to break the parallel path through R2.
Step 4Set the DMM to Ω, with black in COM and red in V/Ω. Probe across R1 without touching the tips, using the lowest non-overload range.
Step 5If R1 is not isolated, the meter reads R1 and R2 in parallel, which is less than R1 alone.
Worked Solution
An ohmmeter drives its own small test current through the component and computes the resistance. Any external voltage or parallel path corrupts the reading. Procedure: (1) Open S1 and remove B1, since a powered circuit can damage the meter and gives false readings. (2) Isolate R1 by lifting one of its leads, so that R2 no longer forms a parallel path. (3) Select the Ω function, black lead in COM and red lead in V/Ω. (4) Place the probes across R1's ends without touching the metal tips, because your body resistance would add another parallel path. Select the lowest non-overload range. (5) Read the display and compare with the nominal value. If R1 is left connected, the meter measures R1 in parallel with R2. The meter's current splits between both resistors, so the displayed resistance is lower than R1.
Problem 11
Ch. 2 — Meter Fuse and Jack Selection
You need to measure the current drawn by a heating element connected to a $24\ \text{V}$ DC supply. The element's resistance is $47\ \Omega$. Your DMM has a mA jack protected by a $400\ \text{mA}$ fuse and a 10 A jack protected by a $10\ \text{A}$ fuse. Using $I = V/R$, estimate the expected current before connecting the meter. Decide which jack is safe to use, and explain what would happen with the wrong choice. Also state how the meter must be connected.
Estimate the current, choose the correct jack, and justify the choice on safety grounds.
0.51 A
Step 1Given $V = 24\ \text{V}$ and $R = 47\ \Omega$.
Step 2Estimate the current: $$I = \frac{24}{47} = 0.511\ \text{A} \approx 510\ \text{mA}$$
Step 3Compare: $510\ \text{mA} > 400\ \text{mA}$, so the mA jack's fuse would blow.
Step 4Use the 10 A jack, which has ample margin, with the function set to DC A.
Step 5Connect in series with the power off, then power up and read. Afterward, return the red lead to V/Ω.
Worked Solution
Given: $V = 24\ \text{V}$ and $R = 47\ \Omega$. Expected current: $$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{24\ \text{V}}{47\ \Omega} = 0.5106\ \text{A} \approx 0.51\ \text{A} = 510\ \text{mA}$$ Comparison: $510\ \text{mA}$ exceeds the $400\ \text{mA}$ fuse rating by a factor of about 1.3, so the mA jack would blow its fuse. If the fuse were missing or the wrong type, the meter's internal shunt could overheat and be damaged. The 10 A jack handles $0.51\ \text{A}$ with a wide margin, so use it, with the function switch set to DC A. Connect the meter in series: turn off the supply, break the circuit, insert the meter, and then power up. Afterward, return the red lead to the V/Ω jack.
Problem 12
Ch. 2 — Finding Voltage from Charge and Energy
During a $4.0\ \text{min}$ charging interval, a battery charger moves $7.5 \times 10^{20}$ electrons through a battery and transfers $1.62\ \text{kJ}$ of energy. Use the constant $1\ \text{C} \approx 6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons, $I = Q/t$, and $V = W/Q$. Find the charge moved, the average charging current, and the voltage at which the charger operates. Give the voltage as your final answer.
Find $Q$, $I$, and $V$. The voltage is the final answer.
13.5 V
Step 1Given $n = 7.5 \times 10^{20}$ electrons, $W = 1\,620\ \text{J}$, $t = 240\ \text{s}$.
Step 2Charge: $$Q = \frac{7.5 \times 10^{20}}{6.25 \times 10^{18}} = 120\ \text{C}$$
Step 3Current: $I = 120\ \text{C}/240\ \text{s} = 0.50\ \text{A}$.
Step 4Voltage: $$V = \frac{1\,620\ \text{J}}{120\ \text{C}} = 13.5\ \text{V}$$
Step 5Units check: $\text{C/s} = \text{A}$ and $\text{J/C} = \text{V}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $n = 7.5 \times 10^{20}$ electrons, $W = 1.62\ \text{kJ} = 1\,620\ \text{J}$, $t = 4.0\ \text{min} = 240\ \text{s}$. Charge: $$Q = \frac{7.5 \times 10^{20}}{6.25 \times 10^{18}}\ \text{C} = 1.2 \times 10^{2}\ \text{C} = 120\ \text{C}$$ Current: $$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{120\ \text{C}}{240\ \text{s}} = 0.50\ \text{A}$$ Voltage: $$V = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{1\,620\ \text{J}}{120\ \text{C}} = 13.5\ \text{J/C} = 13.5\ \text{V}$$ Units check: $\text{C/s} = \text{A}$ and $\text{J/C} = \text{V}$.
Problem 13
Integrated — Interpreting a Battery Discharge Log
A battery analyzer logged the cumulative charge delivered by a battery pack in milliampere-hours (mAh), as shown in the exhibit. Find the average discharge current in amperes over the full $1.5\ \text{h}$ test. Then convert the total delivered charge to coulombs, using $1\ \text{h} = 3\,600\ \text{s}$ and $1\ \text{C} = 1\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$. Give the charge in coulombs as your final answer.
Battery discharge log
Time (h)   Cumulative charge (mAh)
0.0        0
0.5        410
1.0        820
1.5        1230
Find the average current in amperes and the total charge in coulombs.
4.43e3 C
Step 1Average current: $I_{avg} = 1\,230\ \text{mAh} / 1.5\ \text{h} = 820\ \text{mA} = 0.82\ \text{A}$.
Step 2Check: each $0.5\ \text{h}$ adds $410\ \text{mAh}$, which also gives $820\ \text{mA}$, so the current was constant.
Step 3Convert the charge: $1\,230\ \text{mAh} = 1.230\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h}$.
Step 4Convert to coulombs: $$Q = 1.230 \times 3\,600 = 4\,428\ \text{C} \approx 4.43 \times 10^{3}\ \text{C}$$
Worked Solution
Average current: $$I_{avg} = \frac{1\,230\ \text{mAh}}{1.5\ \text{h}} = 820\ \text{mA} = 0.82\ \text{A}$$ Each half-hour adds $410\ \text{mAh}$, so the current was constant at $410/0.5 = 820\ \text{mA}$. Total charge: $1\,230\ \text{mAh} = 1.230\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h}$, and $$Q = 1.230\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h} \times 3\,600\ \frac{\text{s}}{\text{h}} = 4\,428\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s} = 4.43 \times 10^{3}\ \text{C}$$
Problem 14
Integrated — Adding Charges with Different Prefixes
Three charge measurements from separate test runs are $Q_1 = 2.5\ \text{mC}$, $Q_2 = 780\ \mu\text{C}$, and $Q_3 = 3.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{nC}$. Convert each to millicoulombs, find the total charge, and report it with correct precision.
Convert each charge to mC and find the total, reported with correct precision.
3.6 mC
Step 1$Q_1 = 2.5\ \text{mC}$ (already in mC).
Step 2$Q_2 = 780\ \mu\text{C} = 780 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C} = 0.780\ \text{mC}$.
Step 3$Q_3 = 3.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{nC} = 3.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{C} = 0.30\ \text{mC}$.
Step 4Add: $$Q_T = 2.5 + 0.780 + 0.30 = 3.58\ \text{mC}$$
Step 5The tenths place limits the sum: $Q_T = 3.6\ \text{mC}$.
Worked Solution
Convert each charge to millicoulombs. $Q_1 = 2.5\ \text{mC}$. $Q_2 = 780\ \mu\text{C} = 780 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{C} = 0.780\ \text{mC}$. $Q_3 = 3.0 \times 10^{5}\ \text{nC} = 3.0 \times 10^{5} \times 10^{-9}\ \text{C} = 3.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{C} = 0.30\ \text{mC}$. Sum: $$Q_T = 2.5 + 0.780 + 0.30 = 3.58\ \text{mC}$$ Precision: $2.5\ \text{mC}$ is known only to the tenths place, so round to tenths: $Q_T = 3.6\ \text{mC}$.
